# Problem 1: Tidyverse — New Zealand

The `nzge` data were supplied as an RDS file because the original `nzelect`
package has been archived. Candidate and Party votes are kept separate in all
calculations.

```{r}
nzge <- readRDS("data/nzge.rds") |>
  as_tibble()

glimpse(nzge)
```

## 1(a) Vote count by year and vote type

```{r}
votes_by_year_type <- nzge |>
  summarise(
    vote_count = sum(votes, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c(election_year, voting_type)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(vote_count))

votes_by_year_type |>
  mutate(vote_count = comma(vote_count)) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Election year", "Vote type", "Vote count"),
    caption = "New Zealand votes by election year and vote type"
  )
```

The largest total is the 2014 Party vote with
`r comma(votes_by_year_type$vote_count[1])` votes. In every election year, the
Party-vote total is slightly larger than the Candidate-vote total.

## 1(b) Party shares of the 2014 Candidate vote

```{r}
candidate_2014 <- nzge |>
  filter(
    election_year == 2014,
    voting_type == "Candidate"
  ) |>
  summarise(
    votes = sum(votes, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = party
  ) |>
  mutate(proportion = votes / sum(votes)) |>
  arrange(desc(proportion))

candidate_2014 |>
  mutate(
    votes = comma(votes),
    proportion = percent(proportion, accuracy = 0.01)
  ) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Party/category", "Votes", "Share of Candidate vote"),
    caption = "2014 Candidate-vote shares"
  )
```

The National Party received the largest share of the 2014 Candidate vote:
`r percent(candidate_2014$proportion[1], accuracy = 0.1)`. Labour was second
with `r percent(candidate_2014$proportion[2], accuracy = 0.1)`. The source data
place informal candidate ballots in the `party` field, so that category is
shown explicitly and remains in the denominator.

## 1(c) Winning party by year and vote type

```{r}
winning_parties <- nzge |>
  summarise(
    votes = sum(votes, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c(election_year, voting_type, party)
  ) |>
  slice_max(
    order_by = votes,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = TRUE,
    by = c(election_year, voting_type)
  ) |>
  select(election_year, voting_type, party) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = voting_type,
    values_from = party,
    names_glue = "{voting_type}_vote_winner"
  ) |>
  arrange(election_year)

winning_parties |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Election year", "Candidate-vote winner",
                  "Party-vote winner"),
    caption = "Winning party for each vote type"
  )
```

Labour won both vote types in 2002. In 2005, National won the Candidate vote
while Labour won the Party vote. National won both vote types in 2008, 2011,
and 2014.

# Problem 2: Tidyverse — Tennis

The 2019 ATP match data come from the assigned
[Tennis Abstract repository](https://github.com/azhou5849/tennis-atp-sackmann-data/tree/master).
Each row is one match; the file contains separate winner and loser columns.

```{r}
matches <- read_csv(
  "data/atp_matches_2019.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

matches |>
  select(
    tourney_id, tourney_name, tourney_date, round,
    winner_name, loser_name, w_ace, l_ace
  ) |>
  slice_head(n = 8)
```

## 2(a) Number of tournaments

```{r}
tournament_count <- matches |>
  summarise(tournaments = n_distinct(tourney_id))

tournament_count |>
  kable(caption = "Number of distinct tournament/event IDs in 2019")
```

There are `r tournament_count$tournaments` distinct tournament/event IDs in
the file. This count includes Davis Cup ties, which each have their own event
ID in the source data.

## 2(b) Players winning multiple tournaments

A tournament champion is identified as the winner of a match whose round is
coded `F` (final).

```{r}
tournament_titles <- matches |>
  filter(round == "F") |>
  count(winner_name, name = "tournaments_won", sort = TRUE)

multiple_title_winners <- tournament_titles |>
  filter(tournaments_won > 1)

multiple_title_winners |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Player", "Tournaments won"),
    caption = "Players who won more than one tournament"
  )
```

Yes. `r nrow(multiple_title_winners)` players won more than one tournament.
The maximum was `r max(tournament_titles$tournaments_won)` titles, shared by
`r str_c(tournament_titles |> filter(tournaments_won == max(tournaments_won)) |> pull(winner_name), collapse = " and ")`.

## 2(c) Do winners have more aces?

Because both ace totals come from the same match, I analyze the within-match
difference, winner aces minus loser aces. Matches missing either ace count are
excluded.

```{r}
ace_differences <- matches |>
  filter(!is.na(w_ace), !is.na(l_ace)) |>
  transmute(ace_difference = w_ace - l_ace)

ace_summary <- ace_differences |>
  summarise(
    matches = n(),
    mean_difference = mean(ace_difference),
    median_difference = median(ace_difference),
    winner_had_more = mean(ace_difference > 0)
  )

ace_summary |>
  mutate(winner_had_more = percent(winner_had_more, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c("Complete matches", "Mean difference",
                  "Median difference", "Winner had more aces"),
    caption = "Within-match ace comparison"
  )
```

I use a one-sided, simulation-based test from the `infer` package. The null
hypothesis is that the population mean difference is zero, against the
alternative that it is positive. This keeps the inferential workflow in the
tidyverse rather than calling a base-R hypothesis-test function.

```{r}
set.seed(506)

observed_ace_mean <- ace_differences |>
  specify(response = ace_difference) |>
  calculate(stat = "mean")

null_ace_distribution <- ace_differences |>
  specify(response = ace_difference) |>
  hypothesize(null = "point", mu = 0) |>
  generate(reps = 9999, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "mean")

ace_test <- null_ace_distribution |>
  summarise(
    p_value =
      (sum(stat >= observed_ace_mean$stat) + 1) / (n() + 1)
  )

tibble(
  observed_mean_difference = observed_ace_mean$stat,
  simulation_p_value = ace_test$p_value
) |>
  kable(
    digits = 4,
    col.names = c("Observed mean difference", "One-sided p-value"),
    caption = "Simulation-based test of winner-minus-loser aces"
  )
```

Winners averaged `r round(observed_ace_mean$stat, 2)` more aces per match.
The one-sided simulation p-value is
`r format.pval(ace_test$p_value, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)`. This is strong
evidence that winners have more aces than losers on average. This is an
association within completed matches; it does not establish that aces alone
cause a player to win.

## 2(d) Highest win rate, minimum five matches

I reshape winners and losers into a common player column, mark each outcome,
and then calculate wins divided by total matches.

```{r}
player_records <- bind_rows(
  matches |>
    transmute(player = winner_name, won = 1L),
  matches |>
    transmute(player = loser_name, won = 0L)
) |>
  summarise(
    matches = n(),
    wins = sum(won),
    losses = matches - wins,
    win_rate = mean(won),
    .by = player
  ) |>
  filter(matches >= 5) |>
  arrange(desc(win_rate), desc(matches))

highest_win_rate <- player_records |>
  slice_max(win_rate, n = 1, with_ties = TRUE)

highest_win_rate |>
  mutate(win_rate = percent(win_rate, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Player", "Matches", "Wins", "Losses", "Win rate"),
    caption = "Highest 2019 win rate among players with at least five matches"
  )
```

Rafael Nadal had the highest win rate: 60 wins in 69 matches, or
`r percent(highest_win_rate$win_rate, accuracy = 0.1)`.

# Problem 3: Visualization — US COVID-19 cases

The data are the assigned
[New York Times state-level rolling averages](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nytimes/covid-19-data/refs/heads/master/rolling-averages/us-states.csv).
The source already supplies seven-day average daily cases and rates per
100,000 population.

```{r}
covid <- read_csv("data/us-states.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

## 3(a) Major and minor spikes

To make “spike” reproducible, I define a peak as a local maximum within a
plus-or-minus 28-day window, after summing the state seven-day averages. Peaks
below 25,000 cases per day are omitted as small fluctuations. A retained peak
is called major when it reaches at least 150,000 daily cases and minor
otherwise.

```{r}
national_cases <- covid |>
  summarise(
    cases_avg = sum(cases_avg, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = date
  ) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(
    local_window_max = slide_dbl(
      cases_avg,
      max,
      .before = 28,
      .after = 28,
      .complete = TRUE
    )
  )

case_peaks <- national_cases |>
  filter(
    cases_avg == local_window_max,
    cases_avg >= 25000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    spike_type = if_else(cases_avg >= 150000, "Major", "Minor"),
    label = str_c(format(date, "%b %Y"), "\n", comma(round(cases_avg)))
  )

spike_counts <- case_peaks |>
  count(spike_type, name = "number_of_spikes")

spike_counts |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Spike classification", "Number of spikes"),
    caption = "Detected national COVID-19 case spikes"
  )
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6.5
ggplot(national_cases, aes(date, cases_avg)) +
  geom_area(fill = "#9ecae1", alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_line(color = "#08519c", linewidth = 0.55) +
  geom_point(
    data = case_peaks,
    aes(color = spike_type),
    size = 3
  ) +
  geom_label(
    data = case_peaks,
    aes(label = label, color = spike_type),
    size = 2.7,
    linewidth = 0.15,
    fill = "white",
    nudge_y = 36000,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Major = "#b2182b", Minor = "#ef8a62")) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "3 months", date_labels = "%b\n%Y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "Eight distinct US COVID-19 case spikes",
    subtitle = "Three peaks meet the ≥150,000 major-spike threshold; five are minor",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Seven-day average daily cases",
    color = "Spike type",
    caption = "Source: The New York Times COVID-19 data; local maxima use a ±28-day window."
  )
```

Under this definition, there are
`r spike_counts |> filter(spike_type == "Major") |> pull(number_of_spikes)`
major spikes and
`r spike_counts |> filter(spike_type == "Minor") |> pull(number_of_spikes)`
minor spikes. The January 2022 Omicron peak is visually exceptional at more
than 800,000 average daily cases, over three times the next-largest peak.

## 3(b) Highest- and lowest-rate states

I restrict “states” to the 50 states plus the District of Columbia. Summing
the daily `cases_avg_per_100k` values across the full period gives an
approximately cumulative, population-standardized rate and permits a fair
ranking across states of different sizes.

```{r}
states_50_dc <- c(state.name, "District of Columbia")

overall_state_rates <- covid |>
  filter(state %in% states_50_dc) |>
  summarise(
    overall_rate = sum(cases_avg_per_100k, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = state
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(overall_rate))

extreme_states <- bind_rows(
  overall_state_rates |> slice_head(n = 1) |> mutate(rank = "Highest"),
  overall_state_rates |> slice_tail(n = 1) |> mutate(rank = "Lowest")
)

extreme_states |>
  mutate(overall_rate = comma(overall_rate, accuracy = 1)) |>
  select(rank, state, overall_rate) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Overall-rate rank", "State",
                  "Summed daily rate per 100,000"),
    caption = "States at the extremes of the overall population-standardized rate"
  )
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6
extreme_trajectories <- covid |>
  filter(state %in% extreme_states$state)

ggplot(
  extreme_trajectories,
  aes(date, cases_avg_per_100k, color = state)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Maine" = "#2c7fb8", "Rhode Island" = "#d7301f")) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "3 months", date_labels = "%b\n%Y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number()) +
  labs(
    title = "Rhode Island's waves were far sharper than Maine's",
    subtitle = "Daily new cases per 100,000 residents, seven-day average",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Cases per 100,000",
    color = NULL,
    caption = "Source: The New York Times COVID-19 data."
  )
```

Rhode Island has the highest overall standardized rate, while Maine has the
lowest. Rhode Island experienced much larger winter surges, especially the
Omicron wave, which peaked above 500 cases per 100,000 per day. Maine's curve
was lower and flatter early in the pandemic, and its recorded peak was only
about 81 per 100,000. The gap is therefore driven not just by one date but by
repeatedly higher and sharper Rhode Island waves.

## 3(c) First five states substantially affected

I define “substantial” as the first date a state's seven-day average reached
5 new daily cases per 100,000. This threshold is high enough to avoid labeling
isolated initial cases as sustained community spread. Territories are excluded
using the same 50-state-plus-DC definition.

```{r}
first_substantial_dates <- covid |>
  filter(
    state %in% states_50_dc,
    cases_avg_per_100k >= 5
  ) |>
  summarise(
    first_substantial = min(date),
    .by = state
  ) |>
  arrange(first_substantial) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

first_substantial_dates |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("State", "First date at or above 5 per 100,000"),
    caption = "First five states to cross the substantial-spread threshold"
  )
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 8
early_trajectories <- covid |>
  filter(
    state %in% first_substantial_dates$state,
    between(date, as.Date("2020-03-01"), as.Date("2020-05-31"))
  )

ggplot(early_trajectories, aes(date, cases_avg_per_100k)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 5, color = "#636363", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(color = "#2b8cbe", linewidth = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(
    data = first_substantial_dates,
    aes(xintercept = first_substantial),
    color = "#d7301f",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = first_substantial_dates,
    aes(x = first_substantial, y = 5),
    color = "#d7301f",
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ state, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b %d") +
  labs(
    title = "The Northeast led the first wave of substantial state-level spread",
    subtitle = "Red markers show the first date the 7-day average reached 5 cases per 100,000",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Daily cases per 100,000",
    caption = "Source: The New York Times COVID-19 data. Scales vary by panel to reveal timing."
  ) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)
  )
```

The first five states were New York (March 21), New Jersey (March 24),
Louisiana (March 26), Massachusetts (March 27), and Michigan (March 28).
Four of the five are in the Northeast/Midwest corridor, supporting the argument
that the first large US wave was geographically concentrated there, with
Louisiana as the notable early Southern exception.
